lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: The Law of Conservation of Energy

pages.body:
Hold a small torch with a new battery. Switch it on and watch the bulb light. Leave it on for a few minutes and then feel the front of the bulb. Later, try the torch again after leaving it on for a very long time.

- Where did the light come from and why did the bulb become warm?
- What do you think happens to the energy in the battery as time passes?

Energy is always being changed from one form to another, yet scientists have found that none of it is ever lost. In this lesson we state the law of conservation of energy, test it with the example of a dry cell and see how it explains energy conversion in real life.

We begin with a clear statement of the law.

pages.title: What the law says
pages.body:
The law of conservation of energy states that energy cannot be created or destroyed. It can only be changed from one form to another. In a closed system, the total amount of energy before a change is equal to the total amount of energy after the change. A closed system is a set of objects that does not exchange energy with the world outside it.

Now we test the law using the dry cell in a torch.

pages.title: The dry cell as an example
pages.body:
A dry cell stores chemical energy in the chemicals inside it. When the torch is switched on, chemical reactions inside the cell change this chemical energy into electrical energy. The electrical energy flows through the wires to the bulb. In the bulb the electrical energy is changed into light energy and heat energy. We want the light, but some energy always appears as heat, which is why the bulb becomes warm.

[[pic: Energy flow diagram. A dry cell labelled chemical energy 100 units, an arrow to the wires labelled electrical energy 100 units, and two arrows from the bulb, one labelled light energy 10 units and the other labelled heat energy 90 units.]]

Suppose the dry cell supplies 100 units of chemical energy. If the bulb gives out 10 units of light and 90 units of heat, the total is 10 plus 90, which is 100 units. The energy at the end is equal to the energy at the start. None has been created and none has been destroyed. The torch seems to lose energy because the heat spreads into the air and is no longer useful, but it still exists.

**Chemical energy to electrical energy to light energy and heat energy**

The dry cell example shows what we mean by energy conversion.

pages.title: Energy conversion
pages.body:
Energy conversion, also called energy transformation, is the change of energy from one form to another. Each time a change happens, some energy usually becomes heat, spreads into the surroundings and is difficult to use again. The total amount of energy is unchanged but the amount of useful energy goes down.

Finally we use the law to explain things we see around us.

pages.title: The law in real life
pages.body:
- A falling mango loses potential energy as it falls and gains the same amount of kinetic energy, apart from a small part that becomes heat through air resistance.
- When you rub your palms together, the kinetic energy of your hands is changed into heat energy, so your hands become warm.
- In a fire, the chemical energy of wood or charcoal changes into heat and light.
- A bicycle that is no longer pedalled slows down because its kinetic energy is changed into heat by friction, not because the energy has vanished.

> **Did you know?** The law of conservation of energy was developed over many years by scientists such as James Prescott Joule, who showed by experiment that mechanical work and heat are different forms of the same thing. The unit of energy, the joule, is named after him.

questions.q: State the law of conservation of energy.
Describe the energy changes that take place when a torch is switched on.
A battery supplies 200 units of energy and the bulb gives out 20 units as light. Calculate how much is given out as heat.
Explain why a ball bouncing on the ground gradually stops bouncing even though energy is conserved.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Everyday Conversions of Energy into Useful Forms

pages.body:
Look around your home or school. Switch on a bulb, listen to a radio, watch a fan turn and notice a solar powered calculator or lamp. Each device is doing something useful with energy.

- Which form of energy goes into each device and which form comes out?
- Which device changes energy in the most surprising way?

We cannot use energy until it is in the form we need. Devices and natural processes change energy into useful forms. In this lesson we study everyday examples of energy conversion and learn to show them as diagrams.

Before looking at examples we learn how to write the changes as a chain.

pages.title: Reading an energy conversion diagram
pages.body:
An energy conversion chain shows the starting form of energy on the left and each new form that follows. The device or process doing the change is placed above or beneath the arrow. For a torch, the chain is chemical energy in the battery, to electrical energy, to light energy and heat energy in the bulb.

We start with common devices.

pages.title: Examples from the home and school
pages.body:
| **Device or process** | **Energy conversion** |
|---|---|
| Torch | Chemical energy in the cell to electrical energy to light and heat energy |
| Electric iron or kettle | Electrical energy to heat energy |
| Radio or loudspeaker | Electrical energy to sound energy |
| Electric fan | Electrical energy to kinetic energy and a little heat energy |
| Microphone | Sound energy to electrical energy |
| Charcoal stove or gas cooker | Chemical energy in the fuel to heat and light energy |
| Solar calculator or solar lamp | Light energy from the Sun to electrical energy |
| Phone charging | Electrical energy to chemical energy stored in the battery |
Next we see how large scale conversions give us electricity.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Examples from power stations and industry

pages.title: Examples from power stations and industry
pages.body:
- Hydroelectric power at Akosombo and Bui. Gravitational potential energy of water in a lake, to kinetic energy of falling water, to kinetic energy of the turbine, to electrical energy.
- Thermal power station. Chemical energy in the fuel, to heat energy, to kinetic energy of steam, to kinetic energy of the turbine, to electrical energy.
- Car engine. Chemical energy in petrol or diesel, to heat energy, to kinetic energy of the car, with some heat and sound energy lost.
- Solar panel. Light energy to electrical energy.

Finally we look at conversions that happen in nature and in our own bodies.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Examples from living things and nature

pages.title: Examples from living things and nature
pages.body:
- Photosynthesis. Light energy from the Sun is changed into chemical energy stored in sugars and starch in the plant.
- Respiration. Chemical energy in food is changed in the body into kinetic energy for movement and heat energy that keeps the body warm.
- Lightning. Electrical energy is changed into light, sound and heat energy.
- Wind turbines. Kinetic energy of moving air is changed into kinetic energy of the blades and then into electrical energy.

[[pic: A set of four energy conversion diagrams. Each shows a device or process, with boxes and arrows for the forms of energy. The four are a torch, a hydroelectric station, a solar panel and a growing plant.]]
We finish by noting that not all the energy in a conversion is useful.

pages.title: Useful energy and wasted energy
pages.body:
In every conversion some energy is changed into forms that are not the ones we want, mostly heat. For a filament bulb, light is the useful energy and heat is the wasted energy. For an electric iron, heat is useful. The more of the energy that ends as the useful form, the better the device is. An LED lamp changes more of its electrical energy into light than a filament bulb, so it wastes less.

> **Did you know?** A traditional filament bulb changes only a small part of its electrical energy into light. Most of the rest becomes heat, which is why the bulb becomes hot to touch. An LED bulb of the same brightness stays much cooler.

questions.q: Write the energy conversion chain for an electric fan.
Describe the energy conversions in a hydroelectric power station.
Name the energy change that takes place in a plant during photosynthesis.
Explain why an LED lamp is better at using electrical energy than a filament bulb.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Conserving Energy for Present and Future Use

pages.body:
In some parts of Ghana, families spend a lot of money every month on electricity, charcoal or gas. Some switch off lights and cook in covered pots, while others leave bulbs and fans on all day.

- Why do you think it matters if energy is wasted?
- What does your family do at home to avoid waste of energy?

So far we have seen that energy in the scientific sense is never lost. In daily life, however, useful sources of energy such as fuel can be used up. In this lesson we study how to conserve energy, meaning to use it wisely so that it lasts longer, and how this helps humans and other living things.

We begin with the reasons for saving energy.

pages.title: Why we conserve energy
pages.body:
- Fossil fuels such as oil, gas and coal took millions of years to form and will not be replaced in a human lifetime.
- Saving energy saves money for families, schools and the nation.
- Burning less fuel produces less smoke and less carbon dioxide, which means cleaner air and less pressure on the climate.
- Using less firewood and charcoal means fewer trees are cut, which protects forests, soil and the animals that live there.
- There will be energy left for the next generation.

Next we list practical ways of conserving energy in different settings.

pages.title: Ways of conserving energy
pages.body:
| **Place** | **Ways of conserving energy** |
|---|---|
| At home | Switch off lights, fans and television sets when not in use. Use LED bulbs. Use natural daylight and fresh air through windows. Unplug chargers after charging. Iron many clothes in one session. Cook with lids on pots and use a cooking stove that wastes less heat. |
| At school | Switch off lights and fans after class. Arrange classrooms to use daylight. Report leaking taps and faulty appliances. Teach learners to be energy monitors. |
| On the road | Walk or cycle for short trips. Share vehicles. Keep engines tuned and tyres at the correct pressure. Avoid sudden acceleration and braking. |
| In industry and farming | Use efficient machines and maintain them. Use solar dryers for crops. Recover waste heat. Use biogas from animal waste for cooking. |

The Energy Commission of Ghana publishes standards and efficiency labels for appliances such as refrigerators, air conditioners and bulbs, so buyers can choose those that use less electricity.

Another way of looking after our energy supply is to use sources that are not used up.

pages.title: Using renewable energy sources
pages.body:
Renewable energy sources are replaced naturally as fast as they are used. They include sunlight, flowing water, wind, plant material called biomass, and biogas. Solar water heaters, solar lamps and solar panels use sunlight directly. A farm that makes biogas from animal waste gets fuel for cooking and also a rich slurry that can be used as fertiliser. Using renewable sources in place of fossil fuels conserves the fuels that remain.

[[pic: Poster style picture of a house and a school with labels pointing to energy saving practices. Include a solar panel, an LED bulb, a covered cooking pot, a switch turned off and an open window for daylight.]]

Finally we summarise who gains when energy is conserved.

pages.title: Benefits for humans and other life forms
pages.body:
- Humans save money, have cleaner air and a more reliable energy supply.
- Forests and wildlife are protected when less wood and charcoal is used for fuel.
- Rivers, lakes and the sea are cleaner when fewer fossil fuels are drilled, shipped and burned.
- The climate is better protected, which benefits every living thing.

questions.q: State three reasons why we should conserve energy.
Describe three ways in which a family can conserve energy at home.
Name two renewable sources of energy and state one use of each.
Explain how saving charcoal and firewood helps wildlife.

pages.body:
- The law of conservation of energy states that energy cannot be created or destroyed. It can only be changed from one form to another.
- In a closed system the total energy before and after a change is the same.
- In a dry cell, chemical energy is changed to electrical energy, and then in the bulb to light and heat energy. The total is unchanged.
- Energy conversion is the change of energy from one form to another, and some energy usually becomes wasted heat.
- Examples of conversion include torches, fans, stoves, hydroelectric stations, solar panels, photosynthesis and respiration.
- Conserving energy means using it wisely so that sources last longer.
- We can conserve energy by switching off appliances, using efficient devices, using renewable energy and changing habits.
- Conserving energy benefits humans, forests, wildlife and the climate.
